Yes. Rights are an inherent property of sentience. As fully sentient beings endowed with Reason and free Will, we automatically possess certain rights that, while they can be abused and abridged, cannot be taken away from us; but because we have Reason and free Will, we can choose to give them away.

In order that we should not suffer under a state of barbarism, free people can choose to give up some of their rights and enter civil society. In exchange, the Government of a society agrees to compensate its People for the rights they have given up, by guaranteeing certain other (artificial) rights, or by providing certain protections for the rights the People have retained. This exchange is called the "social contract".

Sometimes people violate the social contract by exercising rights they were supposed to have given up. When this happens, the Government punishes those people, because they have committed a crime: they have violated the rights of others.

Sometimes Governments violate the social contract by abusing or abridging rights the People haven't given up, or by failing to live up to its promises of protection or the guarantee of artificial rights. When this happens, the People can revoke their consent to live under their present Government (which at that point has become criminal), and they can alter or abolish the Government, and institute new Government if they wish; and the methods employed in such alteration or abolition don't need to be limited just to the ways that the Government has allowed itself to be reformed. When the Government violates the social contract, the People have the right to enforce the terms of that contract by any means necessary.

Yes, but I agree with Proudhon that property is not a natural right.

To sum up: liberty is an absolute right, because it is to man what impenetrability is to matter, — a sine qua non of existence; equality is an absolute right, because without equality there is no society; security is an absolute right, because in the eyes of every man his own liberty and life are as precious as another’s. These three rights are absolute; that is, susceptible of neither increase nor diminution; because in society each associate receives as much as he gives, — liberty for liberty, equality for equality, security for security, body for body, soul for soul, in life and in death.

But property, in its derivative sense, and by the definitions of law, is a right outside of society; for it is clear that, if the wealth of each was social wealth, the conditions would be equal for all, and it would be a contradiction to say: Property is a man’s right to dispose at will of social property. Then if we are associated for the sake of liberty, equality, and security, we are not associated for the sake of property; then if property is a natural right, this natural right is not social, but anti-social. Property and society are utterly irreconcilable institutions. It is as impossible to associate two proprietors as to join two magnets by their opposite poles. Either society must perish, or it must destroy property.

If property is a natural, absolute, imprescriptible, and inalienable right, why, in all ages, has there been so much speculation as to its origin? — for this is one of its distinguishing characteristics. The origin of a natural right! Good God! who ever inquired into the origin of the rights of liberty, security, or equality? They exist by the same right that we exist; they are born with us, they live and die with us. With property it is very different, indeed. By law, property can exist without a proprietor, like a quality without a subject. It exists for the human being who as yet is not, and for the octogenarian who is no more. And yet, in spite of these wonderful prerogatives which savor of the eternal and the infinite, they have never found the origin of property; the doctors still disagree. On one point only are they in harmony: namely, that the validity of the right of property depends upon the authenticity of its origin. But this harmony is their condemnation. Why have they acknowledged the right before settling the question of origin?

Absolutely natural rights exist.

However, civil rights, which do depend entirely on a government's actions, also exist. A good example of this is, "If you cannot afford one, an attorney will appointed for you."

Note that there is no natural right to an attorney, any more than there is a natural right to health care. Natural rights do not require another human being to go to any sort of grad school. However, court-appointed attorneys are a crucial (if poorly implemented in practice) element of all citizens receiving equal treatment under the law...which isn't a natural right either, since natural rights by definition predate laws.

I would encourage you to wrestle with this concept as you refine your own thinking.

Yeah, I agree that there are universal human rights.

But to possibly answer OP's question, it's not the responsibility of the US federal government to secure those rights for everyone in the world.

Also some things, which some people think are rights, aren't actually rights. E.g., you are free to speak but no one is compelled to listen or give you the spotlight. No one has to respect or approve of you. You should be free to dissociate/emigrate from any anywhere but that doesn't mean that you'll be welcomed/received in the destination of your choosing. You don't have the right to a contract with any particular terms of your choosing (even if you've paid your union dues). No one is required to bake you a cake, or run a fiber optic cable to your front door, etc.

Further, if you commit the right crimes, you can surrender your very right to life itself. If enough evidence condemns you, you can be sentenced to the electric chair, shot on the battlefield or interrogated very harshly (e.g., towards prosecution of your accomplices).

In summary, while I don't want my government going out of their way to violate the rights of non-citizens, there have been cases where rights abuses have been decried and I've been less concerned.
